tagline: Gold towns and dredge tailings below a high mountain crossing
intro: The Elkhorn Drive Scenic Byway makes a 106-mile loop through forests, gold towns and the mountain country west of Baker City. Oregon’s transportation department presents the scenic byway as a journey through gold booms and ghost towns, with three to five hours of driving. The route reaches 7,392 feet at Elkhorn Mountain Summit, while the Anthony Lake approach rises steeply from the Baker Valley. Phillips Lake occupies part of the Powder River corridor, while the upper loop reaches the North Fork John Day River. Near Anthony Lake, jagged peaks form the backdrop to the recreation area before the road drops toward the valley.

Gold discoveries in 1862 brought miners to Granite, and a narrow-gauge railway reached Sumpter in 1897. The railway carried freight for ranchers, mines and timber companies, linking Sumpter with Baker City and Prairie City. Mining also reshaped the ground beside the later scenic drive: Chinese miners stacked larger boulders along Granite Creek, and dredges left fields of disturbed earth near Sumpter.

For a circuit beginning on the valley side, climb from the Baker Valley to Anthony Lake and Elkhorn Summit, then continue toward Granite. Cross Blue Springs Summit to Sumpter, then follow the Powder River corridor past Phillips Lake toward Baker City. U.S. 30 connects Baker City with Haines on the valley side of the loop.

moments.title: Elkhorn Summit
moments.text: At 7,392 feet, Elkhorn Mountain Summit is the highest point on the byway. The jagged peaks here stand behind the Anthony Lakes Recreation Area. Anthony Lake and Grande Ronde Lake lie within a few miles of one another, with camping and fishing as well as winter skiing and snowmobiling. The lake group also includes Hoffer Lakes, Lilypad Lake and shallow marshes. The road’s high crossing is seasonal: snow often keeps the stretch between Granite and Anthony Lake closed until July. The Elkhorn Crest trail extends 23 miles along the range’s spine, from Anthony Lakes south to Marble Pass.

moments.title: Granite
moments.text: A wartime decision brought Granite’s gold economy to a halt. In 1942, the War Production Board issued Order L-208, closing gold mines so miners would work on metals deemed essential to the war. Granite lost telephone and electric service after the war; its population fell from 86 in 1940 to two in 1960. Telephone service returned in 2000, when the town’s population had grown to 24. Along Granite Creek, rock walls remain from an earlier kind of mining. Chinese miners set the larger boulders aside while searching for gold, leaving those piles beside the creek.

moments.title: Sumpter
moments.text: The dredge displayed at Sumpter worked from 1935 to 1954, operating decades after the fire that destroyed the town’s business district. Sumpter had grown after the railway arrived in 1897, with three newspapers and an opera house. By the 1917 fire, the mines were already declining; the blaze destroyed 12 blocks, and dynamite was used to fight it. The last dredge incorporated parts from the first, which had been idle for ten years. The dredge later processed river deposits with buckets, sorting out gold and discharging waste behind it. Those tailings remain a feature of the drive into Sumpter.
